ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
On a smooth, insulated horizontal plane, two small balls A and B, each with mass $m$, are connected by an insulated light rod of length 2L, forming a system. Ball A carries a positive charge q. The dashed lines MN and PQ are parallel and separated by a distance of 3L. Initially, A and B are at rest on opposite sides of the dashed line MN, which is the perpendicular bisector of the line connecting A and B. The balls are considered as point masses, and the mass of the light rod is negligible. After a uniform horizontal electric field directed to the right is applied between the dashed lines MN and PQ, the system begins to move. If ball B is uncharged, the speed of ball B when it reaches the dashed line PQ is $\sqrt{8gl}$. If ball B is given a certain charge, ball B can move from the position shown in the figure to the dashed line PQ. The Coulomb force between balls A and B is negligible, and both balls are considered as point charges.

1. What is the electric potential difference between the dashed lines MN and PQ?
2. What is the polarity of the charge on ball B, and what is the magnitude of the charge on ball B?
3. After ball B carries the charge mentioned above, what is the time it takes for ball B to pass through the dashed line MN for the second time after the system starts moving?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, two vertical dashed lines are respectively labeled MN and PQ, and the two are parallel; the horizontal distance from MN to PQ is labeled 3L. Between MN and PQ, a uniform electric field E horizontally to the right is drawn. A horizontal light rod connects the small ball B on the left and the small ball A on the right; in the initial state B is on the left side of MN, A is on the right side of MN, and beside A is labeled positive charge q; the problem states that MN is the perpendicular bisector of AB and the rod length is 2L, so when taking MN as x=0, initially x_B=-L, x_A=+L, and during motion x_A=x_B+2L, and PQ is x=3L. Reasoning: First look at when B is uncharged. When only A is in the electric field and is acted on by a force, the system is subject to an external force qE; the total mass of the system is 2m, so the acceleration a=qE/(2m). From x_B=-L to x_B=+L, A goes from x=+L to x=3L, is subject to the electric-field force, and the acceleration distance of the system is 2L; after that A leaves the field, B is uncharged, and the velocity remains unchanged. Therefore the velocity when B reaches PQ satisfies v^2=2a·2L=4aL=2qEL/m. The problem gives v^2=8gL, thus E=4mg/q. The spacing between MN and PQ is 3L, and the electric field is to the right, so the potential of MN is higher than that of PQ, hence U_MN-PQ=E·3L=12mgL/q. Suppose the charge carried by B is Q. Divide by x_B: from -L to 0, only A is in the electric field, a1=qE/(2m)=2g; from 0 to L, both A and B are in the electric field, a2=(q+Q)E/(2m); from L to 3L, only B is in the electric field, a3=QE/(2m). In the problem, “can reach PQ” is treated as just reaching PQ, namely v=0 when x_B=3L. From the segmented-motion energy equation 0=2a1L+2a2L+2a3·2L, obtain a1+a2+2a3=0, namely q+(q+Q)+2Q=0, so Q=-2q/3. B carries negative charge, and the magnitude of the charge is 2q/3. At this time a2=(q/3)E/(2m)=2g/3, a3=(-2q/3)E/(2m)=-4g/3. Find the time of passing MN for the second time. Moving to the right: from -L to 0, t1=sqrt(2L/a1)=sqrt(L/g), and the velocity when passing MN is v1=sqrt(2a1L)=2sqrt(gL). From 0 to L, the final velocity v2=sqrt(v1^2+2a2L)=4sqrt(gL)/sqrt(3), so t2=(v2-v1)/a2=(2sqrt(3)-3)sqrt(L/g). From L to 3L, under a3=-4g/3 it decelerates to zero, t3=(0-v2)/a3=sqrt(3)sqrt(L/g). When returning from 3L to L, it is still subject to a3=-4g/3, accelerating leftward from rest, t4=sqrt(3L/g)=sqrt(3)sqrt(L/g). From L to 0, it is subject to rightward acceleration a2=2g/3, and the initial velocity is -4sqrt(gL)/sqrt(3); solve -L=-(4/sqrt(3))sqrt(gL)t+(1/3)gt^2, take the smaller root for the first arrival at 0, t5=(2sqrt(3)-3)sqrt(L/g). The total time t=t1+t2+t3+t4+t5=(6sqrt(3)-5)sqrt(L/g).
